title: Does AI Help Junior or Senior Developers More?

narration.licence: draft only: unofficial Microsoft Edge read-aloud API, no terms for published media

sentences.text: Picture a pair of developers switching on the same AI coding assistant on the same morning: a veteran, and a newcomer just starting out.

onScreenText: A veteran and a newcomer

sentences.text: Which of them gets more out of it?

onScreenText: Which of them gets more out of it?

sentences.text: The confident answer online is the veteran, so let's put that answer next to the trials that actually measured it.

onScreenText: The confident answer: the veteran

sentences.text: On The Pragmatic Engineer, in an episode about AI at Shopify, it was offered as a maybe: "the AI agents are going to help the best engineers more than the mediocre engineer".

onScreenText: "the AI agents are going to help the best engineers more than the mediocre engineer"

citations.label: The Pragmatic Engineer, episode on AI at Shopify
citations.detail: The Pragmatic Engineer: "How AI is changing software engineering at Shopify with Farhan Thawar" youtube.com/watch?v=u-3IILWQPRM

sentences.text: On the same show, Simon Willison said that with these tools he will "run circles around somebody who's never written a code line of code in their life".

onScreenText: "run circles around somebody who's never written a code line of code in their life"

citations.label: Simon Willison on The Pragmatic Engineer
citations.detail: The Pragmatic Engineer: "AI tools for software engineers, but without the hype – with Simon Willison (Co-Creator of Django)" youtube.com/watch?v=uRuLgar5XZw

sentences.text: Willison's yardstick is someone who has never coded, and the trials that follow compared developers with each other, so what they can test is the first claim: when researchers split their results by experience, did the best engineers gain more than the rest?

onScreenText: Did the best engineers gain more than the rest?

sentences.text: In field experiments that gave developers the coding assistant Copilot, short-tenure developers raised their output by 27 to 39 percent, while long-tenure developers gained 8 to 13 percent.
Those estimates are noisy and not statistically significant, but the pattern was the same on all three of the studies' main output measures.

onScreenText: Noisy, not statistically significant

chart.title: Output gain with Copilot, by tenure
chart.note: Ranges across three output measures; estimates noisy and not statistically significant.

citations.label: Cui et al., Copilot field experiments

sentences.text: The authors note that longer-tenure developers abandoning the tool after a trial may shrink their estimate, yet junior developers, who used it as much as seniors once they had adopted it, still gained more than senior ones.

excerpt.text:
Moving on towards output measures in Figure 6, we see that the productivity-enhancing
effects of Copilot are stronger for lower tenure and more junior developers. While our
estimates are noisy and not statistically significant at conventional levels, the pattern is
the same across all three main outcome measures: short-tenure developers increase their
output by 27% to 39% while long-tenure developers have smaller gains of 8% to 13%.
However, we note that because of our emphasis on the average effect of initially adopting
Copilot and the patterns in Figure 4(a), the estimates for longer-tenure developers may
be attenuated by a larger extent of developers abandoning the technology after an initial
trial phase. Still, there is no difference in usage conditional on adoption between junior
and senior developers in Figure 4(b), and still we see in 6(b) that junior developers in-
crease their output by 21% to 40% while senior developers have more marginal gains of
7% to 16%. The estimates for above and below-median productivity developers are even
noisier but directionally consistent.
excerpt.highlight: no difference in usage conditional on adoption

citations.label: Cui et al., Copilot field experiments

sentences.text: A separate experiment found the same direction: developers with fewer years of experience got the speed benefit from generative AI, while the quality of their code was unaffected.

Another Copilot trial found that less experienced programmers benefited more, and its authors called that promising for people moving into software development, if the result holds up in further studies.

onScreenText: Fewer years of experience: faster, quality unaffected
Less experienced programmers benefited more

citations.label: Shan et al., generative AI experiment
citations.detail: Shan et al. field study + RCT (4859137.txt, lines 872-878)

sentences.text: An experiment that ran from bachelor's students to professional developers found that every group got significantly further through its task with AI support, and its authors say the differences between groups were not related to experience.
Professionals gained more there than bachelor's students, but each group had tasks suited to its level, and the professionals' were among the most complex.

onScreenText: Every group got further with AI
Professionals gained more, on the most complex tasks

citations.label: Code-ownership experiment, BSc students to professionals

sentences.text: Then there is a trial of developers who knew their projects deeply: 5 years and 1,500 commits on average in the repositories they worked on.

chart.title: Average experience in their own repositories

sentences.text: With AI allowed, these developers were slower, not faster, and its researchers report moderate evidence that they were slowed down more on issues where they had high prior exposure to the task; the developers said AI was particularly helpful on unfamiliar issues and less helpful on familiar ones.

excerpt.text:
pleted in the study--this is why we have a smaller number of issues for our baseline slowdown
estimate. See Section D.4 for details on how we estimate heterogeneous treatment effects.

Qualitatively, developers note that AI is particularly helpful when working on unfamiliar issues, and
less helpful when working on familiar ones.

One developer working with unfamiliar datasets found that AI was helpful in answering "general
questions about e.g. EICAR." Another developer noted that Cursor was "super helpful in figuring
out how to write a [frontend test.] I didn't know how to do this before and on my third time asking
cursor for help with it, it came up with this solution." Another developer, working with Git hooks,
noted that "Given that it was my first time with Git hooks, without AI the implementation would've
taken me [3 additional hours]." Sometimes, portions of one's own codebase can be as unknown as
a new API. One developer noted that "cursor found a helper test function that I didn't even know
existed when I asked it how we tested deprecations."

On the other hand, developers note that AI is much less helpful on issues where they are expert. One
developer notes that "if I am the dedicated maintainer of a very specialized part of the codebase,
there is no way agent mode can do better than me."

Broadly, we present moderate evidence that on the issues in our study, developers are slowed down
more when they have high prior task exposure and lower external resource needs. We hypothe-
size that analogously, AI helps our developers less compared to existing literature [10; 11] because
our developers have substantially more experience on their respective repositories (5 years and
1,500 commits on average). This would be consistent with the experience/familiarity effects ob-
served in Noy and Zhang [23]; Cui et al. [17].
excerpt.highlight: less helpful when working on familiar ones

sentences.text: As one developer put it: "if I am the dedicated maintainer of a very specialized part of the codebase, there is no way agent mode can do better than me."

onScreenText: "if I am the dedicated maintainer of a very specialized part of the codebase, there is no way agent mode can do better than me."

sentences.text: One trial leaned the other way: on a complex task, more senior engineers were, if anything, faster with AI than less senior ones, though that difference was not statistically significant.
Its authors suggest AI may not yet be able to close a skill gap on a task that complex.

onScreenText: Seniors faster with AI, not statistically significant
AI may not yet close a skill gap on complex tasks

sentences.text: That leaves the other half of the belief: that using these tools well is a skill of its own, and the skilled pull ahead.

onScreenText: Is using these tools well a skill of its own?

sentences.text: Among those deeply experienced developers, the slowdown broadly did not shrink with up to 50 hours of Cursor experience, counting the hours they reported from before the study.
One developer past 50 hours did see a speedup, but when a second developer corrected the experience they had reported, that group's estimate fell from roughly 25 percent faster to roughly 0 percent.

chart.title: Over 50 hours of Cursor: estimated speedup
chart.note: Experience hours partly self-reported; the group is very small.

sentences.text: In the trial that leaned toward seniors, run with full-time Googlers, how often people already used AI tools made no significant difference to their speed with AI; among the possible reasons its authors offer are too little statistical power, a low usability floor where the benefits come quickly, and one feature needing prompting skills that may not be universal yet.

onScreenText: Prior AI use: no significant difference
Too little statistical power
A low usability floor
Prompting skills not universal yet

sentences.text: The clearest sign that tool skill matters comes from a maintainability trial: the more practised the original developer was with AI, the better the code scored on a code-health measure once someone else built on it, though that developer's proficiency in Java mattered even more.

excerpt.text:
As with the completion time, the Bayesian analysis provides more nuanced insights.
We found that the more AI-skilled the Task 1 participants were, the stronger the effect
of their AI usage on Task 2 CodeHealth. For habitual AI users, the estimated mean
effect was a significant absolute increase of +0.10 in CodeHealth. While the effect may
appear small, we should note that this signal corresponds to half a standard deviation,
detected in an average over about 50 files � and the effect is robust across priors. Still,
building on code developed by a proficient Java developer mattered even more.

    The findings show that developers vary in their ability to work effectively with AI
assistants. While this is not surprising, it suggests that training developers to properly
use these tools remains important in the current AI era. Adding to that, we also

sentences.text: So across these trials, nothing shows AI multiplying experts far more than novices: several leaned toward the less experienced, though the field experiments' gaps were noisy and not significant and another trial's result awaits further studies, and the one hint the other way was not significant either.

What runs through them is how much the developer already knew: the tool helped more for short-tenure developers in one trial and on unfamiliar issues in another, and helped less for maintainers on tasks they knew well.

onScreenText: Nothing shows AI multiplying experts far more
It helped more where the developer knew less

citations.label: Cui et al., Copilot field experiments

sentences.text: But how can a tool that writes code for you leave an expert slower on work they know best?

onScreenText: How can it leave an expert slower on work they know best?

sentences.text: Back with those maintainers, the answer starts with how often they took what the tool offered: they accepted fewer than 44 percent of Cursor's generations.
When they turned one down, they reprompted or gave up, and the researchers saw significant time wasted reviewing, testing or modifying code before rejecting it.

sentences.text: Even accepted code cost time: 75 percent said they read every line the AI wrote, and 56 percent said they often had to make major changes to clean it up.

sentences.text: Engineers deciding when to hand work to Claude described the same trade; for a task under 10 minutes, one said, "I'm probably not going to bother using Claude."
Another described a cold start: their team's codebase holds knowledge Claude does not have by default, so rather than iterate on the perfect prompt, "I'm just going to go and do it myself."

onScreenText: "I'm probably not going to bother using Claude."
"I'm just going to go and do it myself."

sentences.text: The same limit shows up at larger scale: in one company's AI-assisted migration of 5,359 files, the bottleneck was how fast engineers could review the changes, so the team deliberately capped how many changes it generated each week.

onScreenText: Bottleneck: how fast engineers could review

sentences.text: A review of what has been written about vibe coding names its central risk a verification gap: code generated faster than developers and their processes can verify its correctness, security and provenance.
Its authors suggest that skill in verification, constraint specification and review may matter as much as skill in writing code.

onScreenText: A verification gap
Verification and review may matter as much as writing code

sentences.text: And the study of engineers using Claude names the catch, a "paradox of supervision": using Claude effectively requires supervising it, and supervising it requires the very coding skills that may atrophy from overuse.
That checking is part of the price those maintainers paid.

onScreenText: "paradox of supervision"

sentences.text: So before you hand a task to an assistant, ask yourself how much of it you already know, and how long checking its answer will take.
And if you find yourself deleting most of what it writes, point it at the parts that are new to you, and keep enough of the skill to check what it hands back.

onScreenText: How much of it do you already know?
Keep enough of the skill to check what it hands back
